title: “YOU MUST BE BORN AGAIN” — NICODEMUS WAS CONFUSED FOR A REASON
paragraphs: “YOU MUST BE BORN AGAIN” — NICODEMUS WAS CONFUSED FOR A REASON

He Knew the Scriptures. He Lived a Religious Life. He Even Recognized That Jesus Came From God. But One Conversation in the Darkness Exposed the Terrifying Truth: You Can Know Everything About Religion and Still Miss the Life Only Christ Can Give.
He came to Jesus at night.
Not because he had never heard about God.
Not because he was an atheist.
Not because he was living some scandalous double life that everyone in Jerusalem was whispering about.
He came carrying something far more unsettling.
He had spent his life teaching people about God, yet he was standing before the Son of God without understanding how to enter His kingdom.
And perhaps the most frightening part of his story is that millions of people today could be sitting in the very same darkness without realizing it.
They attend church.
They know when to stand, when to bow their heads, when to say amen.
Some have served faithfully for decades.
Some have preached.
Some have led worship.
Some have built entire reputations around being good Christians.
And yet, beneath all that religious familiarity, there is a question that no church attendance record, ministry title, family tradition, or public reputation can answer.
Have you actually been born again?
Not merely inspired.
Not simply improved.
Not emotionally moved by a sermon.
Not baptized into a religious culture while your heart remains untouched by the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
Born again.
Because Jesus did not come merely to make religious people more religious.
He came to give life to people who cannot give spiritual life to themselves.
And that is precisely why Nicodemus was confused.
He was looking at Jesus through the eyes of everything he had learned, everything he had accomplished, and everything he believed made him spiritually secure.
But Jesus was about to tell him something that would shake the very foundation beneath his feet.
Something that should shake ours too.
The Gospel of John introduces Nicodemus with remarkable detail.
He was a Pharisee, a ruler of the Jews, and someone Jesus later called “the teacher of Israel” (John 3:1, 10).
This was not an uneducated man struggling to understand basic religious concepts.
He knew the Law.
He knew the prophets.
He knew Israel's history, covenant promises, and expectations concerning the kingdom of God.
He was respected.
He was established.
He was the kind of man others approached when they wanted answers about Scripture.
And yet he approached Jesus with a confession that revealed both recognition and limitation.
“Rabbi, we know that thou art a teacher come from God: for no man can do these miracles that thou doest, except God be with him.” (John 3:2, KJV)
Notice what Nicodemus acknowledged.
He recognized something extraordinary about Jesus.
He understood that the signs pointed toward God's activity.
But recognizing that Jesus is extraordinary is not the same as recognizing who Jesus truly is.
There are people today who admire Jesus as a great moral teacher.
They appreciate His compassion.
They quote His words about love.
They respect His sacrifice.
They even believe that God was with Him.
But admiration alone is not regeneration.
Respect is not surrender.
Religious curiosity is not saving faith.
Nicodemus began by acknowledging what he thought he knew about Jesus.
Jesus answered by exposing what Nicodemus still needed.
“Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” (John 3:3, KJV)
Imagine hearing those words.
You have devoted your life to studying God's commands.
You have spent years pursuing religious faithfulness.
People look at you as an example of spiritual maturity.
Then Jesus looks at you and says, in effect, that none of your religious achievements can produce the new life necessary to enter God's kingdom.
You must be born again.
Not because the Law of God was defective.
Not because obedience to God was meaningless.
But because human beings are incapable of curing the deepest problem of their own hearts.
Sin is not merely a collection of mistakes that better habits can erase.
It is rebellion against the holy God who created us.
It corrupts our desires, distorts our worship, and separates us from the One in whom true life is found.
A person can learn religious behavior without receiving a new heart.
A person can change outward habits without being reconciled to God.
A person can become admired by a congregation while remaining spiritually dependent on something other than Christ.
And Jesus refused to let Nicodemus mistake outward religious standing for inward spiritual life.
Here is where the original Greek makes the conversation especially revealing.
In John 3:3, the phrase translated “born again” is:
γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν — gennēthē anōthen
The verb gennēthē means “be born.”
The word anōthen can mean “again” or “from above.”
That double meaning matters.
Jesus was not simply describing a second beginning on the same human level.
He was speaking about a birth whose source is above — a new life that comes from God.
The same Greek word, anōthen, is used in John 3:31 to describe the One who comes “from above.”
Nicodemus, however, heard the language of birth and struggled to understand it.
He responded:
“How can a man be born when he is old? can he enter the second time into his mother's womb, and be born?” (John 3:4, KJV)
It is tempting to laugh at his confusion.
How could an educated religious leader misunderstand something so badly?
But perhaps Nicodemus was not the only one trapped inside a familiar way of thinking.
Perhaps we are too.
Because when Jesus speaks about new birth, we often begin imagining things we can do.
Attend more services.
Become more disciplined.
Stop certain habits.
Read more chapters.
Pray longer prayers.
Serve more faithfully.
And those things may have an important place in the life of a disciple.
But none of them can manufacture the miracle Jesus is describing.
You cannot give birth to your own spiritual life.
That is the point.
Birth is not an achievement a child earns.
It is life received.
And spiritual rebirth is not the reward for becoming impressive enough to deserve God.
It is the gracious work of God in a sinner who needs salvation.
That truth is both devastating and beautiful.
Devastating because it strips away our illusion of self-sufficiency.
Beautiful because it means the door of salvation is not reserved for people who have managed to make themselves worthy.
The exhausted mother who feels she has failed her children.
The father who has spent years hiding his private sins.
The young adult who looks confident online but cries when nobody is watching.
The church volunteer who serves everyone while quietly battling bitterness.
The person who has fallen into the same temptation so many times that repentance feels almost impossible.
The believer who wonders whether God could still receive someone who has wandered so far.
Listen carefully.
Your greatest need is not to manufacture a more impressive version of yourself.
Your greatest need is the saving grace of Jesus Christ.
And that grace does not begin with pretending that sin is harmless.
It begins with admitting that we need a Savior.
Jesus continued:
“Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God.” (John 3:5, KJV)
This statement has been discussed by Christians for centuries, particularly concerning its relationship to baptism.

Some Christian traditions understand the water as referring directly to baptism, while others emphasize cleansing promised in the Old Testament. These interpretations should not be carelessly treated as identical.
But the larger biblical context gives us something essential that no faithful reading should overlook.
Jesus was speaking to a teacher of Israel who should have recognized God's promises of cleansing and inward renewal.
Consider Ezekiel 36:25–27.
God promised His people:
“Then will I sprinkle clean water upon you, and ye shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you.”
Then comes the promise that reaches directly into the heart of Nicodemus's conversation:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you.”
And God continued:
“And I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes.”
This is not merely about polishing the outside of a religious life.
This is about God cleansing what is defiled, replacing the heart of stone, and giving His Spirit.
In the Hebrew text of Ezekiel 36:26, the promise begins:
וְנָתַתִּי לָכֶם לֵב חָדָשׁ — venatatti lakhem lev chadash
“I will give you a new heart.”
Look at who performs the action.
God says, “I will give.”
He does not say that His people must first create their own new hearts.
He promises to do what they cannot accomplish through human effort.
And that is why Nicodemus's confusion was so revealing.
He knew the Scriptures, but he had not understood the full significance of the very promises Jesus was bringing into focus.
The kingdom of God requires more than religious credentials.
It requires the cleansing and renewing work of God.
And Jesus was announcing that the promised renewal could not be separated from Him.
This is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because some of us have been trying to negotiate with God using our religious history.
“Lord, I have been in church since childhood.”
“Lord, I was baptized.”
“Lord, I never abandoned my ministry.”
“Lord, I have given offerings.”
“Lord, I have helped people.”
“Lord, I have never done what those other people have done.”
But salvation is not a courtroom where we successfully argue that our good deeds outweigh our sins.
It is the gracious rescue of guilty sinners through the righteousness, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
Our good works cannot erase our guilt.
Our religious reputation cannot cleanse our conscience.
Our family background cannot regenerate our hearts.
And even our deepest tears cannot purchase forgiveness.
Only Christ saves.
Jesus then gave Nicodemus an illustration that was as simple as it was mysterious.
“The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit.” (John 3:8, KJV)
In Greek, the word πνεῦμα — pneuma can mean “spirit,” “wind,” or “breath,” depending on context.
Jesus uses the language of wind to illuminate the work of the Spirit.
You cannot command the wind to appear.
You cannot hold it in your hands.
You cannot manufacture its power.
Yet you can recognize its effects.
Leaves move.
Branches bend.
The atmosphere changes.
Likewise, the Holy Spirit's regenerating work is not something human beings can control through religious performance.
But the new life He gives produces real consequences.
A growing hatred of sin.
A new love for Christ.
A desire for God's Word.
Repentance that is more than regret over consequences.
A willingness to forgive.
A longing for holiness.
A life increasingly shaped by the truth and grace of Jesus.
Not instant perfection.
Not the complete absence of struggle.
Not a claim that every genuine Christian will experience transformation in precisely the same emotional way.
But a real work of God that bears fruit over time.
And perhaps that distinction is exactly what someone reading this needs to hear.
Because you may still struggle.
You may still grieve over old temptations.
You may still have days when your faith feels weak.
But the presence of struggle does not automatically mean the absence of spiritual life.
Sometimes the very grief you feel over sin reveals that you can no longer make peace with what once held you captive.
Still, we must be careful.
Conviction by itself is not proof of regeneration.
Religious emotions are not proof.
Even temporary moral change is not the same as saving faith.
The question is not simply whether you feel bad about sin.
The question is whether you are turning from sin and trusting Jesus Christ as your Savior and Lord.
And if you are wondering whether you can come to Him after everything you have done, remember what Jesus said in John 6:37:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
There is no need to clean yourself up before approaching the One who alone can cleanse you.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come believing His promise.
Nicodemus eventually asked:
“How can these things be?” (John 3:9, KJV)
And Jesus responded:
“Art thou a master of Israel, and knowest not these things?” (John 3:10, KJV)
There is something sobering about that exchange.
Nicodemus was a teacher who needed to be taught.
A religious authority who needed spiritual understanding.
A man familiar with sacred words who needed to hear the Word made flesh.
And Jesus did not leave him with a motivational speech about becoming a better person.
He took him to the heart of salvation.
To an ancient scene in Israel's wilderness.
To a people dying because of sin.
To a strange act of divine mercy.
And ultimately, to the cross.
In Numbers 21:4–9, the Israelites sinned against God and spoke against Him and Moses.
Venomous serpents came among them, and many died.
When the people acknowledged their sin, Moses prayed for them.
God instructed Moses to make a bronze serpent and place it on a pole.
Those who had been bitten were to look at it and live.
It was not the bronze object possessing some independent magical power.
It was God's appointed means through which His promise of deliverance was received.
And Jesus told Nicodemus:
“And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up.” (John 3:14, KJV)
Do not rush past those words.
Jesus was pointing toward His own crucifixion.
The Son of Man would be lifted up.
The sinless One would bear the consequences of sin.
The Savior would be publicly shamed.
The Holy One would suffer under the weight of human wickedness.
And sinners who believe in Him would receive eternal life.
Nicodemus came at night wanting to understand the kingdom.
Jesus pointed him toward a cross.
Because the new birth cannot be separated from the saving work of Christ.
Christianity is not merely the announcement that people need to change.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to accomplish the salvation sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
He lived without sin.
He died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day.
And everyone who truly trusts in Him receives the gift of eternal life.
That is the Gospel proclaimed in passages such as 1 Corinthians 15:3–4, Romans 5:8, and Ephesians 2:8–10.
Then, in the very conversation where Nicodemus struggled to understand spiritual rebirth, Jesus revealed one of the most beloved truths in all of Scripture.
“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.” (John 3:16, KJV)
We have seen that verse printed on shirts.
Displayed on signs.
Quoted at church services.
Shared across social media.
But imagine hearing its truth in the context of that nighttime conversation.
Jesus had just exposed the inadequacy of religious status.
He had spoken about humanity's need for a birth from above.
He had pointed toward His coming crucifixion.
And now He declared the love of God revealed in the giving of His Son.
This is not sentimental love that pretends sin does not matter.
It is holy love that provides a Savior for sinners.
In the Greek text, John 3:16 begins:
Οὕτως γὰρ ἠγάπησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν κόσμον — Houtōs gar ēgapēsen ho theos ton kosmon
“For God so loved the world.”
The word houtōs, translated “so,” points to the manner in which God loved: He gave His Son. The verse also communicates the astonishing greatness of that love.
God's love is not presented as an abstract emotion.
It is demonstrated through the giving of Jesus Christ.
And that gift confronts every attempt to earn salvation through human achievement.
You do not climb high enough to reach God.
God has acted in Christ to save sinners.
You do not purchase eternal life with good deeds.
Eternal life is God's gift through His Son.
You do not become worthy of the cross.
The cross reveals both the seriousness of your sin and the astonishing mercy of God.
The same Jesus who told Nicodemus he must be born again also revealed how eternal life is received: through faith in the Son of God.
And suddenly, Nicodemus's story becomes more than a theological conversation.
It becomes a mirror.
Because there are people reading this who know how to appear spiritually healthy while privately falling apart.
You can smile during worship while your marriage is collapsing.
You can post Scripture while secretly nursing unforgiveness.
You can speak about holiness while feeding a habit you refuse to surrender.
You can encourage others while carrying an unconfessed sin that has slowly hardened your heart.
You can defend Christian doctrine online while becoming increasingly cruel to people made in God's image.
You can know the language of grace without having learned to extend grace.
And you can be so busy maintaining a Christian identity that you rarely stop to examine whether your confidence rests in Christ Himself.
Jesus is not impressed by the mask.
But neither is He confused by what is beneath it.
He already knows.
He knows the jealousy.
The lust.
The dishonesty.
The bitterness.
The secret pride.
The spiritual exhaustion.
The fear of being exposed.
The quiet shame you have carried for years.
And He does not call you to hide more carefully.
He calls you to come into the light.
John 3:19–21 explains that people love darkness rather than light because their deeds are evil, while those who practice the truth come to the light.
That is not an invitation to perform your confession for strangers.
It is an invitation to stop protecting the very darkness from which Christ came to deliver you.
Some sins need to be confessed to those we have wronged.
Some struggles require trusted pastoral care, accountability, or professional help.
But none of us needs to make our private pain a public spectacle to prove that our repentance is genuine.
What matters is that we stop treating secrecy as our savior.
Darkness promises protection.
But darkness cannot give life.
Only Jesus can.
And there is another part of Nicodemus's story that deserves our attention.
John does not tell us that Nicodemus immediately fell to his knees that night and made a dramatic public declaration.
We should not invent a conversion scene that Scripture does not record.
Instead, the Gospel gives us glimpses of Nicodemus later in the story.
In John 7:50–52, Nicodemus challenged the unfairness of condemning Jesus without first hearing Him and understanding what He had done.
He was not yet delivering the kind of public confession we might expect from a bold disciple.
But he was no longer merely asking questions in the darkness.
Then came the crucifixion.
Jesus had been condemned.
His body had been wounded.
The crowds had witnessed His humiliation.
The religious establishment had rejected Him.
And in John 19:38–42, Joseph of Arimathea came to take Jesus' body for burial.
Nicodemus came too.
He brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred Roman pounds in weight according to John's account.
Together, they prepared Jesus' body for burial according to Jewish burial customs.
Think about that.
The man who once approached Jesus at night now appears in the account of His burial.
The teacher who struggled to understand why the Son of Man must be lifted up now stands in the aftermath of that lifting up.
John does not explicitly tell us the precise moment of Nicodemus's regeneration.
He does not record Nicodemus's final testimony.
But the progression is striking.
From a private nighttime conversation.
To a measured defense of fair judgment.
To participation in the burial of the crucified Christ.
His story reminds us that we must not pretend to know everything God is doing in another person's heart.
It also reminds us that encountering Jesus is not something we should dismiss as a passing religious experience.
The truth He speaks demands a response.
And perhaps you have been postponing yours.
Not because you hate Jesus.
But because you are afraid of what surrender will cost.
You are afraid of losing the relationship.
Afraid of admitting you were wrong.
Afraid of leaving the sin that has become familiar.
Afraid of facing the people you hurt.
Afraid of discovering that the religious identity you spent years building was never a substitute for knowing Christ.
But consider what is at stake.
Jesus did not say, “It would be helpful if you were born again.”
He did not say, “You might consider spiritual renewal when life becomes difficult.”
He said:
“Ye must be born again.” (John 3:7, KJV)
The Greek expression is:
δεῖ ὑμᾶς γεννηθῆναι ἄνωθεν — dei hymas gennēthēnai anōthen
“You must be born from above.”
The word dei expresses necessity.
This is not an optional improvement for especially devoted Christians.
This is the need of every human being who would enter God's kingdom.
And notice that the pronoun hymas is plural.
Jesus was speaking to Nicodemus, but the necessity extended beyond Nicodemus alone.
It reaches the religious and the irreligious.
The respected leader and the disgraced sinner.
The person raised in church and the person who has never opened a Bible.
The person with a clean public reputation and the person whose mistakes are known by everyone.
No one is saved by ancestry, status, achievement, or religious performance.
We all need the mercy of God.
And here is the beautiful scandal of grace.
The same Gospel that exposes our inability to save ourselves announces that Jesus Christ is sufficient to save.
The cross does not tell us that sin was small.
It tells us that sin was so serious that the Son of God gave Himself to redeem sinners.
The empty tomb does not tell us that death was imaginary.
It declares that the crucified Savior has risen victorious.
And the new birth does not mean your past never happened.
It means your past does not have to remain your master.
The adulterer can repent.
The proud can be humbled.
The bitter can learn forgiveness.
The dishonest can begin walking in truth.
The spiritually indifferent can awaken to the glory of Christ.
The broken can find mercy.
And those who once trusted in their own righteousness can abandon that false refuge and rest in Jesus.
Not because every earthly consequence disappears.
Not because reconciliation is always immediate.
Not because genuine disciples never stumble.
But because the grace of God does not merely decorate an unchanged life.
It brings us into a new relationship with God and begins transforming us into the likeness of His Son.
As 2 Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
This is the heart of our message.
Not from scandal to religious camouflage.
Not from shame to a better public image.
Not from sin to self-righteousness.
From condemnation to forgiveness in Christ.
From spiritual death to new life.
From hiding in darkness to walking in the light.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the old story never happened, but by redeeming sinners and giving them a new identity in Him.
And if something inside you has been unsettled while reading this, do not immediately bury that discomfort beneath another distraction.
Examine yourself before God.
Not with the hopeless assumption that every weakness proves you are lost.
And not with the careless assumption that years of religious activity guarantee you are saved.
Ask the deeper question.
Am I trusting Jesus Christ Himself?
Have I turned from sin and placed my faith in His death and resurrection?
Is my hope of acceptance before God grounded in His grace, or in the story I tell myself about being a good person?
Do I desire to follow Him, even when obedience exposes what I would rather hide?
You do not need to manufacture an extraordinary emotional experience.
You need the Savior.
And if you recognize your need for Him, you can call upon Him now.
Not because repeating a prayer mechanically guarantees regeneration.
But because the Lord who calls sinners to repent and believe is merciful, faithful, and worthy of your trust.
You can pray from the heart:

“Lord Jesus, I have spent too much time trusting in myself, hiding my sins, and confusing religious activity with knowing You. I confess that I am a sinner and cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Cleanse me. Give me the new life that only Your Spirit can give. Teach me to turn away from sin, trust Your Word, and follow You as my Savior and Lord. I do not want to hide behind religion. I want to belong to You. Amen.”
And if this message has exposed something in your heart, do not let the moment pass without responding.
You do not have to disclose private sins or painful details publicly.
But you also do not have to walk through your spiritual questions alone.
And perhaps this is where the message needs to travel beyond your own screen.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be attending church every Sunday while silently questioning whether they truly know Jesus.
Someone may be exhausted from trying to earn God's acceptance.
Someone may have stopped praying because shame convinced them that God would never receive them.
Someone may have mistaken a religious upbringing for personal faith in Christ.
Not merely to increase the reach of another Christian post, but because the truth of the Gospel is worth bringing into places where people are already listening.
Send it privately to someone who may need the assurance that salvation rests in Christ, not in human performance.
Read them for yourself.
Examine the context.
Let Scripture shape your understanding rather than allowing a powerful emotional moment to become a substitute for biblical truth.
Because discipleship should not end when an article ends.
We need the Word when life is peaceful.
We need the Word when temptation becomes fierce.
We need the Word when grief visits our homes, when marriages face pressure, when doubt becomes loud, and when our hearts are tempted to wander.
That is why Gospel Warrior is committed to helping people go deeper than a passing moment of inspiration.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment, spiritual encouragement, and Christ-centered learning more accessible.
Not because giving money proves that you have been born again.
Not because financial support is a condition for receiving the grace of Christ.
But Scripture does teach that believers may honor God through generous, willing support of faithful Gospel ministry.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be reluctant or forced, because God loves a cheerful giver.
And Philippians 4:15–18 shows how believers participated in the work of the Gospel through practical financial support.
That is the spirit of this invitation.

For those who choose to include ministry support within their personal giving, this may be one way to express generosity. But it should never be presented as a replacement for every believer's responsibilities to their local church, nor as a compulsory biblical tithe.
You should never feel pressured to give beyond your means.
The widow, the student, the unemployed father, the struggling family, and the believer who has nothing financially to spare are no less precious in the sight of God.
You are welcome here.
The Gospel remains free.
Our desire is not to sell salvation.
It is to steward the opportunities God gives us to proclaim the Savior.
These products can serve as everyday reminders of biblical truth, encouragement for your own walk with Christ, or thoughtful gifts for someone you love.
It is participating in a mission that seeks to keep pointing people back to Jesus.
Save the Scriptures we have studied.
Pray that this ministry will remain faithful to God's Word, humble before Christ, and courageous in proclaiming the Gospel.
Because the measure of a Christian ministry is not merely how many people follow its page.
It is whether the truth of Jesus Christ is faithfully proclaimed and whether people are encouraged to know, trust, and obey Him.
One more thing before you go.
Return in your imagination to that quiet night in Jerusalem.
Nicodemus is standing before Jesus.
He has the education.
He has the reputation.
He has the religious experience.
He has the respect of his community.
And yet the Son of God tells him that he needs something no human achievement can produce.
A new birth.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to become someone God could finally accept.
Perhaps you have been measuring your worth by your failures.
Perhaps you have been holding tightly to your religious accomplishments because you are terrified of admitting that you need grace.
Perhaps you are afraid that if Jesus truly knows your heart, He will turn away.
But the Gospel announces something far greater than self-improvement.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ rose from the dead.
Christ calls us to repentance and faith.
And through the work of His Spirit, God gives new life to those who belong to His Son.
Nicodemus came with questions.
Jesus gave him the truth he needed.
And now that truth stands before us.
Not as an invitation to build a more impressive religious image.
But as a summons to abandon every false hope of saving ourselves and place our trust in the crucified and risen Lord.
You can spend your whole life learning how to look alive before people.
But only Jesus Christ can give you life before God.
The greatest tragedy is not that Nicodemus came to Jesus in the darkness — it is that you could hear the same words in the light and still refuse the Savior who came to give you life.
